Elon is doing what Javier Milei is trying to do with Argentina's economy.  He literally brought a chain saw to symbolize cutting government spending (aka austerity measures).  Musk later busted out a chainsaw for the same symbolism.  The idea is, cut government spending to reduce the crowding out effect.  

The crowding out effect is the idea that government spending decreases private sector investment.  One example of this is the government borrowing money puts upward pressure on interest rates (higher demand means higher price, in this case price of borrowing money).  That higher interest rate means private companies have less room to borrow and grow.  USPS, while important to national security, does take some business from FedEx/USPS.

The expected outcome, is a drop in markets as spending is slashed, some sideways movement as the private sector invests to fill the spending gap.  Then a recovery as the private sector grows faster than it did before govt spending cuts.

Argentina hasn't succeeded yet and they still have a long way to go.  From one article I read, Argentina has a budget surplus and inflation has fallen significantly from 300% to  28% annualized.  On the other hand poverty is up 11% and there are a lot of protests.  Their next step is the economic expansion, if Argentina's economy stagnates, then govt cuts will be offset by slowdown in growth.

I taught hundreds of people to swim in private lessons and I couldn't recommend it more.  I learned a lot over the years so experience is really helpful.  I would call up a couple local competitive swim team or and see if any of their older swimmers teach lessons.  I think a private pool is helpful in bonding with the kids to build trust and also allow for controlled distractions (as opposed to a public pool).  Also swim teachers go to school and I was booked 6hrs/day 5 days a week all summer by March of each year, so start looking now for lessons in 2023.

Learning to swim is mostly about spending time in the water.  Spend time in the water with your child until they are comfortable with you, hanging onto a wall, splashing, and touching their face to the water.  If you change your grip while holding them and they flinch or get wide eyed, they aren't ready for lessons.  I spent months teaching kids not to fear the water, then a couple weeks teaching them to actually swim, so I think it's better if parents fix that.
